newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: CRICKET-CONFIDENT AUSTRALIA STILL SHOW SIGNS OF WEAKNESS.
newsitem.headline: CRICKET-CONFIDENT AUSTRALIA STILL SHOW SIGNS OF WEAKNESS.

text.p: When the Australian cricket team board a plane in Sydney on Saturday they will be taking a first step toward more Ashes glory against England.
That, at least, is what some would have Australian fans believe as the unofficial world champions prepare to embark on a 10-week tour of England which includes the six-test series.
After recent series wins over South Africa and West Indies, the Australians have good reason to be confident before the start of the first test at Edgbaston on June 5.
In contrast, England over the same period were beaten in a limited overs series by lowly Zimbabwe and then improved marginally to score a test series win over New Zealand.

But the level of confidence displayed by some of the Australians poses interesting questions. Are they simply indulging in the age-old practice of pom-baiting, or do they genuinely believe little serious opposition awaits them?
Elegant number four batsman Mark Waugh said in an interview for a pre-series tour guide he thought England players were self-centred and lacked toughness.
"I look at the (England) team on paper and think they are good players, but they aren't tough enough or hungry enough on the field," said Waugh, a veteran of 63 tests.
"They don't play as a team, they worry about themselves ... you don't feel you've got 11 guys against you," he said.
Waugh, whose comments are sure to inflame old rivalries, predicted a repeat of Australia's 4-1 win in England in 1993.
Former coach Bob Simpson said in an English newspaper last week England will not win unless they go back to basics.
"England players are making fundamental errors when it comes to judging the length of a ball, or bowling the right length," said Simpson, who was replaced last July by Geoff Marsh.
"Test cricket is about building up pressure over long periods and the only way to do that is to bat and bowl with discipline," he said.
"In 1989 (when Australia won 4-0) we had no masterplan beyond batting with proper technique and patience ... and bowling straight. There was no great secret to it."
The Australians at least have the form to back up the confidence displayed by Waugh and Simpson.

Australia's series-deciding second test win over South Africa in Port Elizabeth in March reinforced their position at the top of the Wisden world championship and came after a 3-2 home series win over West Indies ending in February.
The defeat of the West Indies was more significant because it proved their historic win over the former unofficial world champions in the Caribbean in 1995 was no fluke.
But despite their impressive recent form the Australians still appear to have their weaknesses, with doubts lingering over the future of captain Mark Taylor.
Taylor's well-documented loss of form has seen him go without a test 50 since late 1995, a run of outs during which he coincidentally became one of Australia's greatest test captains.
Taylor will arrive in London on Monday with his position the least secure of all, particularly after wicketkeeper Ian Healy was replaced by Steve Waugh as vice-captain for the Ashes tour.
The feisty Healy was suspended for dissent for two matches during the South African tour and has since promised to be a quieter competitor.
"Just knowing when to speak up or not will be different," Healy recently told reporters. "I've really only got performance pressures now, just like any other player."
Healy's demotion could further weaken Taylor's position as the dour but ultra-competitive Waugh is seen in Australia as a more likely captain than the chatterbox 'keeper.
Taylor himself conceded after the 17-man touring squad was chosen last month that it was possible Waugh could take over from him during the tour if his tortuous form slump continues.
"I am a realistic person. That is a possibility," he said.
Master leg-spinner Shane Warne also had a quiet southern hemisphere summer by his own lofty standards after undergoing finger surgery 12 months ago.
While still Australia's main attacker, Warne is a different bowler to the wunderkind who snared Mike Gatting's wicket with his first delivery in the 1993 Ashes series.

The emergence of middle-order batsman Michael Bevan as a quality leg-spinner has taken a lot of heat off Warne, while the Australians are also still fine-tuning their batting order to accommodate emerging youngsters such as left-hander Matthew Elliott and the mercurial Ricky Ponting.
Australia must now live up to both their formidable reputations and the pre-tour bluster, with the reformed Healy adopting the uncharacteristic role of diplomat.
"They (England) look good on paper again and, as individuals, are very good players who probably haven't played that well as a team in the past," Healy said.
"But if a few of them manage to stand up it could make a big difference," he said.
